They send 3200 a month to a taxable brokerage while barely passing the 401k match, yet each pretax 401k dollar saves at least 22 percent in federal tax. After the match, the usual order is HSA if eligible, Roth IRAs for both, via backdoor if over the income limit, then max both 401ks, then the brokerage. Add a 529 for the kids.

Term life on both, disability insurance for him, and wills naming a guardian should come before either big change. Not financial advice. A fee only planner could stress test the one income plan.

Normally, an IOU is basically: _“Bro, I owe you $10,000. I’ll pay you later.”_ But in your example, the company says: _“We owe you something valuable, but instead of promising to pay you money, we’re promising you a piece of the company or a future company benefit.”_

So imagine you do work for a tiny company that has almost no cash. The company basically hands you a fancy piece of paper saying:

> “We owe you. We can’t pay you properly today, so here’s a contractual right to receive stock/options under these agreed conditions.”

That **stock option is functioning economically like the IOU**, because you're accepting something that represents a future claim rather than receiving cash immediately.

Now crank the circus music up: the IOU doesn't necessarily have to be _money_. It could be a **product, service, discount, future credit, equity, or some other agreed benefit**.

For example, a startup could say: _“We owe you $10,000 worth of consulting fees. Instead of paying $10,000 cash, we'll give you a contractual right to receive 10,000 units of our product later.”_ That's essentially a **private, non-cash IOU**.

The important distinction is that an IOU is fundamentally about an **obligation to deliver something in the future**. What that “something” is—cash, shares, products, services, credits, etc.—depends on the contract.

And if it's **stock options**, that's not literally the same legal thing as a normal IOU: an option is a specific contractual right with conditions, expiration, exercise terms, vesting, and potentially no guaranteed value.

>Death of the spring drive
It's a beautiful movement and watchmaking marvel, but if it breaks say 20 years from now you're FUCKED, Seiko will refuse to fix it. If anything malfunctions in the movement, no one can help you. Whereas a traditional mechanical movement can be worked on and maintained by any independent watchmaker, the Spring Drive is only serviceable by GS. It's already happened, the very first Spring Drives released in 1999 GS will refuse to fix, and nobody else can.
Beyond that, you should be sending your watch in for servicing every 10 years minimum. They recommend 5-7 years officially but fug that 10 is fine. If you don't service it for lubing it'll slowly wear down, you need lube on the gears to prevent friction to prevent the gears from grinding down into dust which WILL happen if you don't service it regularly, akin to an oil change in a car. If you can't afford $1,000 every decade for upkeep, you shouldn't consider a mechanical watch.
Assuming you buy a "nice used one" you should immediately ship it to GS for servicing if you plan to wear it for any decent length of time unless the seller provides servicing records. Also, the slga007 is so much nicer with the gold logo and seconds hand imo.
